comments.author: jboggan
comments.textRawHtml:
I was a graph theory junkie long ago and even moved to Budapest for awhile to study among the greats. While I was there I started working on Barnette's Conjecture which came to occupy my thoughts over the next 24 years of my life, on and off as I worked in many different fields. Last summer I even thought for a few days that I had actually solved it.

But it's supposedly proven here - problem 180. I don't know what to think exactly. I spent thousands of hours on that problem. I really enjoyed it. Hearing that it is solved somehow makes me sad in a far-off way, like hearing an ex-girlfriend died suddenly in a car crash. I don't know, there's probably a lot of people feeling odd emotions tonight.

There's no Lean proof for this one so I'm digesting the paper. On the surface it looks like an approach I considered 24 years ago and abandoned.

I revisited the problem this summer, along with my partial solutions, when the previous round of stunning proofs came out. Several hours of work with Fable simply convinced me it wasn't yet solvable and reinforced how hard of a problem it was.
comments.textZhHtml:
我很久以前就是一个图论迷，甚至搬到布达佩斯一段时间来向伟人学习。当我在那里的时候，我开始研究巴尼特猜想，在我接下来的 24 年里，随着我在许多不同领域的工作，它时断时续地占据了我的思想。去年夏天，我什至想了几天，我实际上已经解决了它。

但据说它在这里得到了证明 - 问题 180。我不知道到底该怎么想。我在这个问题上花费了数千小时。我真的很喜欢它。听到这个问题以某种方式解决了，我感到一种遥远的悲伤，就像听到前女友在车祸中突然去世一样。我不知道，今晚可能有很多人感到奇怪的情绪。

这个问题没有精益证据，所以我正在消化这篇论文。从表面上看，这似乎是我 24 年前考虑过但后来放弃的方法。

今年夏天，当上一轮令人惊叹的证明出来时，我重新审视了这个问题，并提出了我的部分解决方案。在《神鬼寓言》中几个小时的工作让我确信这个问题尚无法解决，并强化了这个问题的难度。

children.author: nilkn
children.textRawHtml:
> Several hours of work with Fable simply convinced me it wasn't yet solvable and reinforced how hard of a problem it was.

This is the part that gives me the strangest feeling about it all, because you're not the only one with this experience. I've experienced this too on different problems, as have many researchers across many fields.

I disagree with the Fields Medalists on the majority of their complaints. AI math is happening and there's no going back. However, on one point I increasingly agree: virtually none of this stuff is possible with technology any normal citizen has access to. I have no problem with AI models making revolutionary advances in math or science. Where I start to have a problem is when the AI models making these advances are tightly withheld, proprietary, and seemingly never released with these capabilities intact. This has been the case for all of 2026 so far.

I suspect that this is in fact the source of much of the angst. None of this progress is reproducible outside of one or two teams inside OpenAI and Anthropic. It's becoming an incredible concentration of power that I don't know that we've ever quite seen before. Right now, it feels harmless because it's being used for wonky math problems that aren't (yet) practical for anything. But great power never stays harmless. History has taught us that countless times, in countless different forms.
children.textZhHtml:
> 几个小时的《神鬼寓言》工作让我确信这个问题还无法解决，并强化了这个问题的难度。

这部分给了我最奇怪的感觉，因为你不是唯一有这种经历的人。我在不同的问题上也经历过这种情况，许多领域的许多研究人员也经历过这种情况。

我不同意菲尔兹奖得主的大部分抱怨。人工智能数学正在发生，而且没有回头路。然而，有一点我越来越同意：对于任何普通公民都可以使用的技术来说，几乎所有这些事情都是不可能的。我对人工智能模型在数学或科学领域取得革命性进步没有异议。我开始遇到的问题是，取得这些进步的人工智能模型被严格保留、专有，而且似乎从未在完整发布这些功能的情况下发布。到目前为止，2026 年的情况都是如此。

我怀疑这实际上是大部分焦虑的根源。这些进展在 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 内部的一两个团队之外都无法复制。它正在变得令人难以置信的权力集中，我不知道我们以前见过这种情况。现在，它感觉无害，因为它被用于解决不可靠的数学问题，而这些问题（尚）对任何事情都不实用。但强大的力量永远不会无害。历史无数次以无数不同的形式告诉我们这一点。

children.author: omnicognate
children.textRawHtml:
> I suspect that this is in fact the source of much of the angst.

Why do you "suspect" this as if it's some hidden motivation when the very first paragraph of the advisory group's statement (linked from the OpenAI post) says:

> At present, some frontier AI labs are testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models that remain inaccessible to the broader scientific community. Our recommendations are formulated with this practical context in mind. However, ideally, they would not do so. We want to state clearly from the start: we do not endorse this practice, and we ask them to stop testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models.

Tao and others in that group have been strongly and publicly pro AI from the start. They are not advocating "going back". They're objecting to the strip mining of open problems using proprietary technology.
children.textZhHtml:
> 我怀疑这实际上是大部分焦虑的根源。

当咨询小组声明的第一段（链接自 OpenAI 帖子）说：

> 目前，一些前沿人工智能实验室正在专有模型上测试高级数学问题，而这些模型仍然无法被更广泛的科学界所接受。我们的建议是根据实际情况制定的。然而，理想情况下，他们不会这样做。我们想从一开始就明确表示：我们不认可这种做法，我们要求他们停止在专有模型上测试高级数学问题。

Tao 和该小组中的其他人从一开始就强烈公开支持人工智能。他们并不是提倡“回去”。他们反对使用专有技术对开放问题进行露天开采。

children.author: fasterik
children.textRawHtml: I don't think the strip mining metaphor is appropriate. Mining is a zero-sum game; if I mine something, nobody else can go and mine the same resources I did. Mathematical problems don't go away when AI finds a Lean proof. They create new opportunities for humans to study the solutions, learn new techniques from them, identify promising directions for future research, discover alternative/more beautiful proofs, and write expositions for other humans.
children.textZhHtml: 我认为露天采矿的比喻并不合适。挖矿是一种零和游戏；如果我开采了一些东西，其他人就无法开采与我相同的资源。当人工智能找到精益证明时，数学问题并不会消失。他们创造新的人类有机会研究解决方案，从中学习新技术，确定未来研究的有希望的方向，发现替代/更漂亮的证明，并为其他人撰写阐述。

children.author: MarkusQ
children.textRawHtml: Strip mining is very apt if you view the economics of the present system as "effort -> recognition -> career advancement".  Even in strip mining, the resources that had been buried are now available for use in the broader economy.    What's no longer available is the living that was to be had digging them out.
children.textZhHtml: 如果您将当前系统的经济学视为“努力 -> 认可 -> 职业发展”，那么露天采矿是非常合适的。  即使在露天采矿中，埋藏的资源现在也可用于更广泛的经济。    不再可用的是那些将它们挖出来的活人。

children.author: fasterik
children.textRawHtml: The problem isn't effort, though. All of the things I mentioned constitute effort and could be rewarded. The job economy was created by mathematicians incentivizing the proof of difficult theorems above all else and valuing all other work at approximately zero as far as career advancement was concerned. Now they're pulling a 180 and claiming that math was never really about proving theorems, but that's contradicted by their revealed preferences. The strip-mining problem only exists if they continue with the status quo ante.
children.textZhHtml: 不过，问题不在于努力。我提到的所有事情都是努力并且可以得到回报的。就业经济是由数学家创造的，他们将困难定理的证明置于一切之上，并就职业发展而言将所有其他工作的价值近似为零。现在他们却一百八十度大转弯，声称数学从来就不是证明定理的真正目的，但这与他们所揭示的偏好相矛盾。仅当他们继续保持原状时，露天采矿问题才会存在。

children.author: vector_spaces
children.textRawHtml:
Mathematicians aren't homogeneous. There are mathematicians valuing pedagogy, collaboration, bridge-building, theory building, along with those that chase the 'difficult theorems', to name a few, and there are lots of flavors within each class, with lots of blending and blurring. You infer that mathematicians prefer the status quo simply because it is the status quo -- with a little thought, you'll recognize that this is a fairly silly notion.

There are myriad circumstances where the values of most practitioners differ from the status quo, which is nevertheless well-entrenched. This can arise from inertia, or from outside forces, such as broader cultural milieu, integration with larger institutions, or contending with economic realities. If you think that these do not and haven't historically played a role in determining the job economy and that math is a pure field where mathematicians could comfortably shape it according solely to their own ideals then you are naive
children.textZhHtml:
数学家并不是同质的。有些数学家重视教学法、协作、桥梁建设、理论建设，还有那些追求“困难定理”的数学家，仅举几例，每个班级都有很多风格，有很多混合和模糊。你推断数学家更喜欢现状，只是因为它就是现状——稍加思考，你就会认识到这是一个相当愚蠢的想法。

在很多情况下，大多数从业者的价值观与现状不同，但现状却根深蒂固。这可能源于惯性，也可能源于外部力量，例如更广泛的文化环境、与更大机构的整合，或者与经济现实作斗争。如果你认为这些在决定就业经济方面过去没有、也没有发挥过作用，并且数学是一个纯粹的领域，数学家可以完全根据自己的理想轻松地塑造它，那么你就太天真了

children.author: impendia
children.textRawHtml:
And, in addition, many mathematicians are graduate students or postdocs hoping to line up a permanent job soon.

For example, if you look at Terry Tao's blog, he has a tremendous amount of first-class expository writing. So, too (to some extent) do junior mathematicians -- but, unfortunately, this tends to not be highly valued by the job market. Grad students and postdocs have learned that to succeed they need to play by the existing rules of the game.

Well, the board has just been yanked from underneath them. People like me can afford the sort of idealism and soul-searching that the parent comment describes, but junior mathematicians face a very unenviable set of circumstances.
children.textZhHtml:
此外，许多数学家都是研究生或博士后，希望很快就能找到一份长期工作。

例如，如果你看看陶哲轩的博客，你会发现他有大量一流的说明文写作。 （在某种程度上）初级数学家也是如此——但不幸的是，就业市场往往不高度重视这一点。研究生和博士后已经了解到，要取得成功，他们需要遵守现有的游戏规则。

好吧，木板刚刚从他们下面被拉了出来。像我这样的人可以承受家长评论中描述的那种理想主义和反省，但初级数学家面临着非常的一系列情况。

children.author: MarkusQ
children.textRawHtml:
1) I never said the problem was effort; I was trying to explain the strip mining analogy, and it's one of the two anchors that make the analogy work.

2) Mathematicians didn't create this economy; it was foisted upon them by the same managerial mentality that brought us "publish or perish" and "the monthly sales quota".

3) I can't tell if you honestly don't get why the strip-mining analogy resonates, or...?

Here's another analogy: if we suddenly discovered personal teleportation, and marathon runners were complaining that it was ruining the sport, would you say "they're pulling a 180 and claiming that marathon running was never really about getting to a point 26 miles away as fast as possible, but that's contradicted by their revealed preferences"?

The strip mining analogy is better though, because it captures the sense of irreversible goal-loss when a problem goes from being "unsolved" to "solved".
children.textZhHtml:
1) 我从来没有说过问题在于努力；我试图解释露天采矿的类比，它是使类比有效的两个锚点之一。

2）数学家并没有创造这种经济；他们创造了这种经济。这是由同样的管理心态强加给他们的，这种管理心态给我们带来了“出版或灭亡”和“每月销售配额”。

3）我不知道你是否真的不明白为什么露天采矿的类比会引起共鸣，或者......？

这是另一个类比：如果我们突然发现个人传送，马拉松运动员抱怨它正在破坏这项运动，你会说“他们来了个 180 度大转弯，声称马拉松跑步从来都不是为了尽可能快地跑到 26 英里外，但这与他们所揭示的偏好相矛盾”？

露天采矿的类比更好，因为它捕捉到了当问题从“未解决”到“已解决”时不可逆转的目标损失的感觉。

children.author: fasterik
children.textRawHtml:
As far as I understand, even with "publish or perish", peer reviewers decide what counts as an important enough paper to be published in a prestigous journal, and committees of peers decide whether or not, say, an expository article on arXiv or a textbook counts toward hiring or tenure. Again, as far as I understand, those things have largely not been rewarded in the past.

I like your marathon example, but maybe not for the reasons you intended. The community of marathoners decides the rules of a marathon. You don't need a hypothetical teleporter; you're already not allowed to use a bicycle, performance-enhancing drugs, or shoes that don't fit the specifications. The rules are updated to adapt to changing technology. Yes, I'm arguing that the strip-mining analogy doesn't make sense because mathematics is in the same situation. There's nothing stopping peer reviewers and hiring/tenure committees from changing the rules about which kinds of effort confer recognition and career advancement.
children.textZhHtml:
据我了解，即使是“发表或灭亡”，同行评审员也会决定什么才是足够重要的论文，可以在知名期刊上发表，而同行委员会则决定 arXiv 或教科书上的说明性文章是否算作聘用或终身教职。再说一遍，据我所知，这些事情在过去基本上没有得到回报。

我喜欢你的马拉松例子，但可能不是出于你想要的原因。马拉松运动员社区决定马拉松比赛的规则。你不需要一个假设的传送器；你需要的是一个传送器。你已经被禁止使用自行车、兴奋剂或不符合规格的鞋子。规则不断更新以适应不断变化的技术。是的，我认为露天采矿的类比没有意义，因为数学也处于同样的情况。没有什么可以阻止同行评审员和招聘/终身教职委员会改变有关哪种努力可以带来认可和职业发展的规则。

children.author: orand
children.textRawHtml: Are you advocating to unionize advanced mathematics??
children.textZhHtml: 您是否主张建立高等数学工会？

children.author: MarkusQ
children.textRawHtml:
NO. Most definitely not. Nor am I advocating any sort of gatekeeping.

My entire point is that there is a legitimate perspective, held by real people, from which the "strip mining" analogy is perfectly apt. There were fishermen working these waters for many generations before the trawlers came, and they see the situation differently than the people who've got a vested interest in the company running the factory fishing operations.
children.textZhHtml:
不。 绝对不是。 我也不提倡任何形式的把关。

我的全部观点是，存在着由真实的人持有的合法观点，“露天采矿”的类比是非常恰当的。 在拖网渔船到来之前，这里的渔民已经在这片水域工作了好几代，他们对形势的看法与那些在工厂化捕捞作业公司中拥有既得利益的人不同。

children.author: Catloafdev
children.textRawHtml:
Strip mining is an extraordinarily appropriate metaphor.

Imagine a mine has an unknown number of rare materials. And you know the general location of a few of the most valuable spots. But you don't know what may be valuable right next to it. If the pieces that we know are valuable are suddenly gone, the incentive to mine that particular area drops considerably, dropping the chance to discover potentially brand new materials that would have been found the normal way.
children.textZhHtml:
露天开采是一个非常恰当的比喻。

想象一下一个矿井里有数量未知的稀有材料。您还知道一些最有价值的地点的大致位置。但你不知道旁边可能有什么有价值的东西。如果我们知道有价值的碎片突然消失了，那么开采该特定区域的动力就会大大下降，从而失去发现以正常方式发现的潜在全新材料的机会。

children.author: fasterik
children.textRawHtml: That's an empirical claim. I could equally well say that doing an automated search of the problem space and having a database of results and open problems will identify vastly more interesting and valuable areas. Again, the idea that math is some exhaustible material is a metaphor, not an established fact. I'm willing to change my view as new evidence comes in, but I think we're going to have to wait and see what the landscape looks like in a few years.
children.textZhHtml: 这是一个经验主义主张。我同样可以说，对问题空间进行自动搜索并拥有结果和开放问题的数据库将识别更加有趣和有价值的领域。再次强调，数学是某种取之不尽用之不竭的材料的想法只是一个比喻，而不是既定的事实。随着新证据的出现，我愿意改变我的观点，但我认为我们将不得不等待，看看几年后的情况会是什么样子。

children.author: AnIrishDuck
children.textRawHtml:
> the incentive to mine that particular area drops considerably, dropping the chance to discover potentially brand new materials that would have been found the normal way.

FWIW, I think the metaphor breaks down with this framing. This isn't really a problem associated with strip mining, what's left behind is generally low or negative value (toxic). I'd suggest a different metaphor, from Wikipedia:

> This process involves the removal of all ground vegetation in the area, which is a detriment to the environment.[19] Topsoil may be placed over the tailing along with planting trees and other vegetation. Another reclamation method involves filling in the hole with water to create an artificial lake. Large tailing piles left behind may contain heavy metals which can leach out acids such as lead and copper and enter into water systems.

This feels very similar to the issues with algorithmic problem "mining". It has the potential to destroy the human ecosystems surrounding these problems, leaving barren wasteland behind where nothing can grow or flourish.
children.textZhHtml:
> 开采该特定区域的动机大大下降，从而降低了发现以正常方式发现的潜在全新材料的机会。

FWIW，我认为这个比喻在这个框架下崩溃了。这实际上并不是与露天采矿相关的问题，留下的东西通常是低价值或负值（有毒）。我建议使用维基百科的一个不同的比喻：

> 这个过程涉及清除该地区的所有地面植被，这对环境有害。[19]表土可以覆盖在尾矿上，同时种植树木和其他植被。另一种填海方法是将洞中注水以形成人工湖。留下的大型尾矿堆可能含有重金属，这些重金属可以滤出铅和铜等酸并进入水系统。

这感觉与算法问题“采矿”的问题非常相似。它有可能破坏围绕这些问题的人类生态系统，留下任何东西都无法生长或繁荣的贫瘠荒地。

children.author: hex4def6
children.textRawHtml:
I hope sincerely hope they don't currently use "proprietary technology" like:

Wolfram Mathematica ($890/yr)

Magma ($2500/yr)

Maple ($680/yr)

COMSOL ($1500,yr)

Matlab ($500+/yr)

Seems like a very strange position to take, in my opinion.

Why does the field of mathematics suddenly now need to be "fair" and give everyone access to the same tools? Has that ever been the case in academics? It's always been a competition for name-recognition, grants, institutions, etc.

Macsyma / Maxima was an MIT developed CAS system back in the 60's that was proprietery until they sold it off to IBM for a tidy sum. Magma actually has free access if you're in the US, otherwise you pay. That's not to mention proprietary MATLAB toolboxes or specialized Stata modules.

Likewise, a lot of the above packages have pretty sweet site-wide deals with R1 universities. If you're at a smaller, foreign one, you're out of luck.
children.textZhHtml:
我衷心希望他们目前不要使用“专有技术”，例如：

Wolfram Mathematica（890 美元/年）

Magma（2500 美元/年）

Maple（680 美元/年）

COMSOL（1500 美元/年）

Matlab （每年 500 美元以上）

在我看来，这似乎是一个非常奇怪的立场。

为什么数学领域现在突然需要“公平”并让每个人都能使用相同的工具？学术界曾经有过这样的情况吗？这一直是一场关于知名度、资助、机构等的竞争。

Macsyma / Maxima 是麻省理工学院在 60 年代开发的 CAS 系统，在他们以可观的价格将其出售给 IBM 之前，它一直是专有的。如果你在美国，Magma 实际上可以免费使用，否则你需要付费。更不用说专有的 MATLAB 工具箱或专门的 Stata 模块。

同样，上述许多软件包都与 R1 大学达成了相当不错的全站协议。如果你在一家较小的外国公司，那你就不走运了。

children.author: tancop
children.textRawHtml:
You can't compare that to a model that cost tens of millions to train, millions more to run, and if you don't work at OpenAI you can't get it at all no matter how much you're willing to pay.

Everything about it is secret. There is no API access or official model card that could tell you how it works. You don't know how it came up with the results, how much time it had to spend, if it's a pure LLM or a neuro symbolic AI or a human in the loop system that still needs hundreds of trained mathematicians. Math always cared about transparency (maybe except Stephen Wolfram) and this is the complete opposite.

And because they don't share reasoning traces or anything at all other than finished results, no one knows how much credit really belongs to them. It's perfectly possible that their system is searching the internet for promising leads, connecting them all together to build a coherent proof and then completely throwing away the sources.

I don't think it works like that but no one can know for sure because they never show us what it's really doing.
children.textZhHtml:

One interesting fact I've heard recently (I live in Poland; we share a border with Ukraine as well as with a part of Russia).

Russia went all in on "digital sovereignty." This is partly because the Russian government cares deeply about censoring what their citizens can see (which they can't do if those citizens consume content from American services), partly because the American services themselves cut Russia off because of sanctions-related concerns.

This makes Russian datacenters a much more attractive target for the Ukrainians. While Russia can (and does) bomb Ukrainian datacenters, the fact that Ukrainians are so reliant on US infrastructure (and could rapidly move local workloads to western clouds if the need was great enough) makes such operations far less attractive. It's much easier for Ukraine to strike some facility near Moscow than it is for Russia to strike Ashburn, Virginia.

Given the geopolitical concerns from both the east and the west, this makes the question of whether Europe should move content off of US infrastructure a lot more complicated.

The second order effect will be that rental properties are driven from places where this applies.

That has some not-fun generational aspects.

(1) If schools have lower taxes, their ability to attract good educators for children is reduced. That in turn leads to lower home values since the school quality factor is reduced.

(2) If munis are unable to collect a sufficient tax base, they must reduce services. There will be hemming and hawing about things like cutting the pensions promised decades ago to attract competent service workers, but those are harder to reduce rather than not fixing the fire trucks, the water pipes, and other hidden taxes citizens pay for by reduced services. So your property values will also be reduced in the long term. Small towns are prime examples of this happening, when towns fail.

Trying to build a community out of one socioeconomic class works about as well as trying to redline. It leads to a less vibrant community, less adaptable community, and people are poorer in life and in their finances for it.

Glancing at the Touhou 4 decomp[1], it's a lot better quality than a lot of AI decomps I've seen. It's matching, the variables are named sensibly, comments are sparse and comprehensible, and there's not much in the way of unaddressed Ghidra jank. And only in a month! My main complaint is that the file structuring seems more optimized for AI use than for mirroring the original intent of the devs. (Compare to this human-made Touhou 6 decomp.[2])

I know the retro game modding/decomp scene is already getting hit with a flood of low-effort ports.[3] Now they're going to be hit with a flood of half-decent decomps effortlessly generated by anyone with a $200/mo AI subscription, which become half-decent PC ports, which get modding support grafted on. It kinda just... totally eliminates that as a hobby entirely. I know people are going to be upset about this. And it's not even like with the AI art, where the pro and anti-AI camps live in their own camps. Solving the same puzzle twice just feels discouraging. Very similar to the problem academics are having with AI math/physics proofs.

I know a large reason people hate AI is because it's largely seen as tearing apart hobbyist/professional communities, eliminating reasons to collaborate with others and form relationships, and replacing it with an individualized dependence on a commercial product. It follows the same trend the tech industry took social media, from a method of connection to a tool of propaganda and paranoia and "@gork is this true?" This project, I think, is one of the most clear examples of that.

Compared to that, whistle was really bad (out of 170 messages, qwen recognized correctly 168, whistle - 70), but I adjusted whistle to work like jev - instead of free form transcription it recognizes only select set of templates (I trained tiny network with 10,000 generated utterances to translate whistle final state to probabilities within templates). The precision went up to 164/170 - almost matching qwen. By the way - I'm speaking with heavy accent.

WSDL - now that's a name I've not heard in a very long time!

XML Web Services were awesome, but the SOAP and XML (where the hard parts that should have been given some batteries included defaults) I think was too much of a boat anchor to overcome.

And then the ruby/rails wave came and made 'rest' JSON the Silicon Valley hearthrob, and WSDLs were out like yesterdays trash.

Are they still used in businesses IRL? Yes! I worked for one that has probably (probably) moved off of them by now, but as recently as 2023 there were still some bank-facing power with SOAP RPC .asmx endpoint servers.

I follow hypermedia.systems and htmx/datastar/alpine.js because I'm still trying to get back that powerful _web_ tech advancement rather than squeezing everything into the javascript client side workaround. Typescript is great, a good poor man's F# and leagues ahead of ES3 (which I dabbled in / torture LLMs with so my old retrocomputers can still do web things), but its still bringing along so much baggage that could be lighter weight for older devices AND fits the tech utopianist promise of the original web (which is half of why I play with computer stuff).

children.author: miki123211
children.textRawHtml:
Poland runs on WSDL, SOAP, XML Schema, XSLT, XML Forms, all of it.

By law, every single government form you're able to file is supposed to have an XML Schema available in a centralized registry. This regulation is widely ignored in practice, particularly by local / municipal governments.

This used to be more important in the past, as such a form could automatically / semi-automatically get an entry in the EPUAP form catalog and be made electronically fillable (EPUAP being the now-deprecated centralized government bureaucracy portal basically). As far as I understand, the way that worked was through XSLT and XML Forms. There was some weirdness about each document having a fillable / form view and a preview, I think XML Forms was somehow used to generate the XHTML form, while the XSLT sheet could only generate an XHTML preview of a complete, filled-in version. There were also some custom annotations for auto-fill and such, that was partly done by most documents relying on standardized schemas for entities like "person", "address" or "company".

Since we moved to E-Deliveries and lost a central place for these forms to live in, this is (AFAIK) a bit less important and less common, but internally, things are still XML. If you're filing something like an ID renewal application, even through a newer, more user-friendly frontend, it's still just XML underneath. If you sign something through podpis.gov.pl (the standardized e-signature solution for government paperwork), you can even download that underlying document, both signed and unsigned, and see what that XML is. The pre-signing document preview generated by that site still comes from the XSLT I believe. The signatures themselves are, unsurprisingly, also done via the XML signatures spec.

Incidentally, the European E-Delivery system itself also relies on XML, WSDL and Soap pretty heavily. For those unfamiliar and/or not in Europe, it's basically "email but for the government", with all the guarantees and legal obligations of physical mail, cryptographically-attested confirmation of receipt, proper identity verification and assurance, cross-provider address portability, deployed to a lesser or greater extend in many EU countries and set to replace physical mail.
